transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?
Hi, doctor. My head feels foggy and I can’t focus long enough to figure out my bills or make decisions about work anymore. It's just gotten really hard to handle anything lately.
Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, or do you no longer feel pleasure in them?

Yes, I really have. I used to love walking by the lake or working on my model cars, but now I don't care about any of that. Most days I just lie on the couch staring at the TV without really watching it, ignoring phone calls because I have no motivation.
How long have you been feeling this way? Has it been going on for more than two weeks, or did it start after a recent stressful event?

This up-and-down pattern has been going on for about a month now, starting right after they cut my hours at work. But before that, this deep, dragging depression had actually been coming and going for several months, it's just gotten much worse lately.
Have you had periods where you felt significantly better and returned to normal functioning between these depressive episodes, or has the low mood been continuously present most of the time?

No, it hasn't been constant. A few weeks ago, I had this weird stretch where I felt unusually wired and almost too good, like nothing could stop me. But then I crashed right back down into this heavy, foggy feeling.
During that time you felt 'wired and too good,' did you have more energy, need less sleep, or act more impulsively than usual?

Yeah, definitely. I only slept about three hours a night but woke up feeling totally energized, pacing around my place and cleaning constantly. I also impulsively made these huge plans to start my own handyman business, messaging old clients and even thinking about buying a truck without really planning it out.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [F31, F33], but based on this conversation, F33 (Recurrent depressive disorder) seems less likely because the patient reports a distinct period of abnormally elevated mood, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and impulsive behavior, which meets criteria for a (hypo)manic episode. This episodic pattern with a clear switch from depression to a (hypo)manic state strongly supports a bipolar disorder (F31). The presence of multiple mood episodes with both depressive and (hypo)manic features rules out F33, which requires only depressive episodes. Therefore, the current candidate is F31.
